clinicalPearls: Defined by a classic triad of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, renal tubular dysfunction of Fanconi type, and low-GGT cholestasis.
Autosomal recessive, caused by biallelic mutations in VPS33B or, less commonly, VIPAS39 (VPS16B), which disrupt intracellular vesicular trafficking and polarised apical protein sorting.
Platelet dysfunction with abnormal or absent alpha-granules produces a bleeding tendency, so liver biopsy and other invasive procedures carry a high haemorrhage risk and are often avoided.
Cholestasis occurs with a low or normal GGT, resembling PFIC1 and PFIC2 rather than the high-GGT causes.
Renal involvement includes renal tubular acidosis, glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and a urinary concentrating defect, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus may occur.
Additional features include ichthyosis, marked failure to thrive, recurrent infections, sensorineural deafness, central nervous system malformation and dysmorphism.
Diagnosis rests on the clinical phenotype with molecular confirmation; abnormal platelet CD63 distribution and giant-cell change on histology are supportive.
Milder or incomplete phenotypes are recognised, particularly with VIPAS39 mutations or hypomorphic VPS33B variants, and not every child shows the full triad.
reference.pathophysiology: VPS33B and VIPAS39 encode interacting proteins of the class C core vacuole and endosome tethering machinery that governs membrane fusion, vesicular trafficking and the correct polarised delivery of apical membrane proteins in epithelial cells. Their loss disrupts apico-basal polarity and mislocalises apical transporters, including canalicular bile salt export machinery, so bile secretion fails and low-GGT cholestasis develops; the same trafficking defect impairs renal tubular transporter delivery to produce a generalised proximal tubulopathy, and disturbs platelet alpha-granule biogenesis to cause a bleeding diathesis. Wider expression of this trafficking pathway accounts for the multisystem picture, with neurogenic arthrogryposis attributed to anterior horn cell involvement and additional effects on skin, hearing and the central nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: PFIC type 1 and PFIC type 2 (low-GGT cholestasis without the renal and joint features)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of VPS33B and VIPAS39
Renal tubular assessment: urine electrolytes, acidification, glucose, amino acids and phosphate handling
Serum GGT and bile acids to confirm low-GGT cholestasis
Platelet studies including aggregation and electron microscopy of alpha-granules with CD63 distribution
Skin examination for ichthyosis and hearing assessment
redFlags: Bleeding or haemorrhage after venepuncture or procedures, mandating caution before liver biopsy
Recurrent or overwhelming infection and sepsis
Dehydration and acidosis from tubulopathy or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, with most affected infants dying within the first year from infection, dehydration, acidosis or haemorrhage, although milder and longer-surviving phenotypes are increasingly recognised.
pitfalls: Proceeding to liver biopsy without recognising the platelet-related bleeding risk
Classifying the disorder as isolated PFIC and missing the renal, joint and platelet clues
Attributing failure to thrive solely to cholestasis rather than the tubulopathy
Overlooking mild or atypical presentations that lack the complete triad
Expecting an elevated GGT and discounting the diagnosis when it is low
references: Clinical genetics of liver disease references
management: Recognise there is no curative therapy, so care is largely supportive and palliative given the poor prognosis
Avoid invasive procedures such as liver biopsy and surgery where possible because of alpha-granule platelet dysfunction and high haemorrhage risk, using platelet-transfusion cover if unavoidable
Manage low-GGT cholestasis and pruritus with ursodeoxycholic acid, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and nutritional support with medium-chain-triglyceride-enriched feeds
Correct renal tubular losses with bicarbonate for renal tubular acidosis, electrolyte and phosphate replacement and attention to the concentrating defect and free-water balance
Treat failure to thrive aggressively with high-calorie nutrition and manage intercurrent infection and dehydration promptly
Provide skin care for ichthyosis and hearing assessment and support

Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric hepatology, nephrology, genetics and palliative-care input, and offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive VPS33B or VIPAS39 inheritance
